The Mayor of Mobile, like the Mayor of Savannah, has issued his proclamation taking grounds against vigilance committees and the practice of mob lynching, so much resorted to in the South. This is a timely movement. If the Cotton States intended to set up a Southern confederacy, their people must first discipline their minds to submit to law. Without a greater respect for the law, they can establish no popular government at all. The despotism of the sword will follow the despotism of the mob, and the people lose their liberty through their license.

spellchecked_text: THE REIGN OF TERROR SOUTH. Letter from a Minnesotan in New Orleans—The Murder of the Three Carpenters at Friar's Point. True! The St. Anthony News of the 3rd published a letter from Alderman McHerron of that city, who was recently in New Orleans in relation to the treatment received by himself and another Minnesotan, and Northerners generally, in the South, and confirming the atrocious murder of the three carpenters at Friar's Point, Mississippi. The News says: The wife of Ald. McHerron, this city, received yesterday the following letter from her husband, who is now in Cincinnati. It adds another to the list of outrages with which the press is teeming. It is difficult to appreciate the intensity of mingled fear and hate and madness which pervade a community where such outrages are permitted. Mr. McHerron is a well-known citizen of St. Anthony. Mr. Coggs well was recently Deputy Sheriff for this county. There may be some in this community debased enough to betray these gentlemen to the peril of their lives, but we are happy not to know them! I will now give you a brief history of the causes that led me to come to this place, and will in the first place state briefly that it was to save my life. There is a reign of terror in New Orleans, as well as in the whole South. A Northern man holds his life in his hands after getting below Memphis, but nothing to what it is below there. After getting as far as Vicksburg, a Northern man is abused on the smallest pretense imaginable, and if there is a gin house or other building burnt, from any cause whatever, the cry is raised that it is the work of an abolitionist, and woe to the Northern man that is found in the neighborhood. If he escapes being hung, he will be shaved on the head, and branded on his cheek or forehead. If the punishment is meant to be light, he may be tarred and feathered, rode on a rail, and then started to the nearest place to a steamboat or the cars, being abused all the way and started North on deck passage, and if he has no money, to depend on the charity of those he may happen to be with to keep from starving. This is no overdrawn picture, but it does not picture half the enormities practiced by the chivalry of the South. There have been scores of men lynched and hung in the South from no other cause than being Northern Republicans. Although other charges, such as exciting slaves, and giving them poison and arms and ammunition to kill their masters with, are trumped up against them. The matter of hanging three men at Friar's Point, you have no doubt seen in the papers, also a denial of it afterwards by the Southern press, as also that the letter purporting to be written by Halle giving the account of it was a forgery. But I tell you that it is verily believed, a fact, that those three men were hung as stated, but they wish to cover that like the others. You don't hear of one case in fifty that is perpetrated. The policy of the press in the South is to suppress the publication of these things, and when they are published it is the exception rather than the rule. It is a truly horrible state of affairs. In New Orleans there is not even an allusion made to what has been done there, and yet I can furnish proof, if any statement is doubted, that there were, the week before I left, six men hung for being abolitionists, as all Republicans are called, in the city of New Orleans. There have been scores without limit driven from the city by the vigilance committee, so styled. I am, or rather, was informed while in New Orleans that the course taken by those guardians of Southern rights and Southern honor is to ascertain former residence and then write to the subservient tools of the South in the North to find out what the man's politics have been, and if he has been honest enough to act a Republican, he gets his notice to leave instanter. The usual limit is twenty-four hours, and it was on a request of that kind that I left—choosing to leave rather than run the risk of being taken out the next night and hung to a lamp post. You may think such things strange, but nevertheless they are true. I could not write to you to warn you not to write me anything politically that would compromise me, fearing that the letter would be opened and read, thereby precipitating the very thing I was anxious to avoid. But I am thankful that your own good sense guided you in the matter and that you avoided all things of the kind. There were several of my letters opened; some of them were resealed and some had written on the envelope "opened by mistake by another person." Amongst that number, the one you wrote me immediately after election, but you had the information so worded, calling them Black Republicans, that there could be no advantage taken. Mr. G. Coggs well was also driven away. He was notified at eleven o'clock on Saturday night to leave on Sunday. He could not arrange his business by the time the train went out on Sunday evening, and was positively hid until 1 o'clock next morning and then left. He had been to St. Louis, and only got back to New Orleans on the evening he was notified to leave. Doesn't it seem hard that such things should exist in this country? Yet such is the case. I would have remained in New Orleans this winter had I not been interfered with. But it would have been foolhardy in me to have resisted or not complied with their "very moderate request." S.S.F. Time does take the buckram out of all the saintly gentry, etc.

The lynchers took a vote on the subject, and when the fatal hat came round, Finch dropped into it his ballot, inscribed with the word "Death." On counting the ballots, a majority were found to have declared that the culprits should die, and Kelso and his comrade were accordingly hung to a neighboring tree. Young Finch, after witnessing their dying struggles, went home, when his mother anxiously asked him if the thieves had been caught. "Yes," he told her, "and hung, and he had voted to hang them." His mother sadly and solemnly told him he had no right unlawfully to take that which he could not give—the life of a fellow being—and continued a few moments speaking of the enormity of the act. He then left her and went out to plough, but after ploughing a few furrows, he tied his horse, took off one of the reins, and with it hung himself to the lower limb of a tree. When found, his knees almost touched the ground, and he evidently could have arisen to his feet at pleasure had he changed his purpose before insensibility supervened. All attempts to restore the unhappy youth to life proved useless. The affair produced considerable feeling among the members of the vigilance committee.

from Col. Whitman to his son, dated June
End.


1t showed all day June lst, at Virginia
city. Nothing remarkably new in the way
of discoveries. The town was growing
senSibly duller. Many were leaving and Indi
an troubles deferred people from coming in.
Provisions high and scarce. A vigilance
committee was about organizing to lynch
a butcher, but it was promptly nipped In
the bud.


In reference to the war the Colonel SAYS,
unless help in the way of provisions etc. is
furnished by California the volunteers must
disband and the whole fighting given up to
two hundred regulars on foot, in which
event he fears depopulation of the Terri
tory, as the signs of long and bloody war
are imminent. Unless the American troops
can meet the savages in few DAYS and
give them severe lesson in a great battle,
the worst is anticipated When leaving
Virginia City, Col Hays told his troops
that unless they were willing to live on
meat for some time, the road was open to
to Carson City and they were at liberty to
take it. Not man left.


great battle was expected to come off
on Sunday last. The Col says Nevada
and Sierra came nobly to the relief of their
brethren IN Utah; Sacramento did some
thing, but not more than enough to pay for
stolen horses. San Francisco, with mil
lions at stake had done nothing.

 State Items.

 The steamer Sea Bird arrived on the Sd inst, from Los Angeles, bringing intelligence of new ly discovered placer diggings, located about five miles beyond the Tejon upon the river Possi- uncua. The yield is from $4 to $25 per day, to the man.

 Capt. Harry Love, we'll known as the captur- CT of the celebrated robber, Joaquin, was mar lied on the 31st of May last, to Mrs. Mary Ben nett, of Santa Clara.

spellchecked_text: FROM WASHOE.—We have seen a letter from Col. Whitman to his son, dated June 3rd. It showed all day June 1st, at Virginia City. Nothing remarkably new in the way of discoveries. The town was growing sensibly duller. Many were leaving, and Indian troubles deterred people from coming in. Provisions high and scarce. A vigilance committee was about organizing to lynch a butcher, but it was promptly nipped in the bud. In reference to the war the Colonel says, unless help in the way of provisions, etc., is furnished by California, the volunteers must disband and the whole fighting given up to two hundred regulars on foot, in which event he fears depopulation of the Territory, as the signs of a long and bloody war are imminent. Unless the American troops can meet the savages in a few days and give them a severe lesson in a great battle, the worst is anticipated. When leaving Virginia City, Col. Hays told his troops that unless they were willing to live on meat for some time, the road was open to Carson City and they were at liberty to take it. Not a man left. A great battle was expected to come off on Sunday last. The Colonel says Nevada and Sierra came nobly to the relief of their brethren in Utah; Sacramento did something, but not more than enough to pay for stolen horses. San Francisco, with millions at stake, had done nothing. Correspondence of the Herald. WILKES-BARRE, Pa., 9th August, 1856. Messrs. The prominent, and by far the most conspicuous feature of the California news is the prevalence of what would be called on this side of the continent the supreme authority of Judge Lynch. In San Francisco, it is the execution of the decrees of the Vigilance Committee of Five Hundred (not quite so ceremonious as the old Venetian Council), in the prompt punishment of criminals, and for the preservation of law and order. Strange as it may sound in this longitude, these off-hand trials and summary executions are, in good faith, designed for the preservation, rather than the restoration, of law and order. The criminal may be a murderer, a horse thief, burglar, an incendiary, a common shoplifter, or petty rogue; if the Vigilance Committee catch him and convict him, he is instantly carried out and hung up at the nearest convenient tree, or beam, or rope and tackle. The crime, the pursuit, the apprehension, the indictment, the trial, the judgment, and the execution, may all take place in the same afternoon. The whole business, in the case of Jenkins, was done in the course of an evening, by moonlight; and in the case of Stuart, another Botany convict, tried also as a thief, the interval between the commencement of his trial and the hanging was about five hours. In the case of the Mexican woman at Downieville—who, for fatally stabbing a miner, was tried by the popular process in such cases established, and convicted of murder—the blood of her victim was not yet cold, when the woman, having been tried, convicted, and condemned, was swinging lifeless in the air. The Anglo-Saxon institution of the rope, by a sort of 'charter of popular justice,' or 'course of summary judgment,' may be considered as pretty well established in California; but the rapidity with which it brings the criminal to his quietus is somewhat startling to a community accustomed to the slower formalities of law. This quickness of the penalty is even more astounding to our preconceived notions than the rapidity of crimes which come under the death penalty by the new California code. We have no nice distinction between murder and manslaughter, nor between highway robbery and a petty theft: the same judgment of strangulation makes short work of them all. Truly, this is a terrible state of things and is deeply to be deplored. But the people of California, it appears, not only have reasonable excuses for these summary and indiscriminate executions, but their situation is such as imperatively to demand them. spellchecked_text: THE EXECUTION OF JENKINS.—The sudden, unusual, and solemn occurrence which transpired during the night of the 10th instant and the succeeding morning produced throughout our city yesterday a feverish state of excitement. The assumption of authority by a body of respectable citizens, the enforcement of a sentence of death upon a condemned murderer in the dead hour of night, without the usual forms of law, may well create an unusual stir in any community. Deprived of the benefit of laws, and powerless to compel their enforcement, our citizens have been at the mercy of organized gangs of the worst villains that infested our city and preyed upon its inhabitants. Our citizens have been robbed and murdered, our fair city destroyed by the torch of the incendiary, and hundreds of honest young men stripped of their hard-earned gains and their prospects in life ruined. Such a state of affairs could no longer be borne. Against every principle of self-preservation and forbearance, patience and mercy had absolutely ceased. The time had arrived when the people were compelled for the safety of their lives and the protection of their property to take the law into their own hands, and inflict terrible punishment upon the guilty. Extraordinary circumstances justify extraordinary measures and the administration of punishment. The first act in the drama has been enacted, and the felon has paid with his life the penalty of his crimes. We have never been advocates of mob lynch law, snatching from the hands of legal tribunals the powers legitimately conferred upon them, of depriving any of the benefit of a fair and impartial trial by his fellow-men. Yet, in the present condition of municipal affairs, we cannot conscientiously condemn the people for the course they have felt themselves compelled to adopt. Deeply deploring the occasion for the exercise of such acts, we admit that necessity absolutely demanded the assumption of power. The trial and conviction of Jenkins was not the act of an inflamed and excited mob. His case was adjudged with calmness and deliberation, his guilt fully established, and the penalty of death imposed by a body of men respected and esteemed by their fellows, assuming the responsibility imposed upon them by necessity, with a full perception of their accountability to their fellow-men and their Maker. Who but He shall adjudge and condemn them? We dare not. There may be difference of opinion—there is, undoubtedly, as to the punishment of burglary and petty larceny.

On the 6th, Richard McFarland, of Baltimore. THE MARKETS.—Previous to the fire there was an improved demand for all kinds of goods. The fire, however, has tended much to unsettle the market, but there still remains a fair demand from the interior. The supply of breadstuffs is large. Bricks are in fair request at $30 for common to $50 per 1,000 for fine. Coal is dull at $14.

spellchecked_text: THE LYNCH LAW EXECUTERS IN CALIFORNIA. It is to the New York Commercial Advertiser. It will be remembered that when first the intelligence reached us that a so-called "vigilance committee" had been formed at San Francisco on Lynch-law principles, and that, instead of endeavoring to make the courts purer and more efficient, the committee assumed to be independent of and superior to the law and its officers, we deprecated the whole movement as containing the very essence of anarchy and misrule, as in fact substituting violence and an irresponsible authority for recognized institutions with officers amenable to the people. We saw in that step the introduction of a principle that sooner or later must work mischief—for principles are indestructible and operative, and must produce results. The emergency of the case was pressed upon us, and we were told that in no other way could life and property be protected; that the committee were all honorable; that the popular sentiment was entirely with them—a fact which was undoubtedly true at one time, but now proved untrue, as shown by the hideous longing for an exception evinced by the populace when Whitaker and McKenzie hung. The ground assumed in these columns with reference to the vigilance committee system was, that it was wrong in principle, and therefore eventually become evil in practice; that the assumption of authority vested elsewhere by the people, and by them legitimately transferred to the vigilance committee; that it was not merely a local Patton of magical and executive power, but a violent opposition to the laws and constitution of the State, a despotic administration of life and death, of unheard-of punishments, and of "Star Chamber" examinations and convictions—all tending to demoralize and debase the people, by making them familiar with summary convictions and executions without the show of mercy and forbearance or decent ceremony. The last narrative that we published of one of these executions was truly horrifying, and more than justified our censures and prophecies. Its effect upon the community, as described by an independent writer (a citizen of San Francisco) "Two of the vigilance committee have alienated from them some of their best friends, as well as a large majority of this community. You have already heard of the execution by this committee of Whitaker and McKenzie on Sunday. Suffice it to say that that horrid deed has so shocked this community that confidence in the humanity and prudence of the committees has yet to be restored. This community contends if they were so wanting in vigilance as to permit the authorities to take the prisoners from them, they should have let them pass and determined to be careful in future; but this breaking into the prison, and in a spirit of retaliation upon the authorities, hanging these guilty men on Sunday is an outrage which the better part of the community cannot be made either to sanction or tolerate. This committee will hereafter only be commended for any lawful efforts which they may use in bringing criminals to justice, but the time is past when this community will permit them to become judges and executioners." Another move which has already rendered the committee unpopular is an effort on the part of many of its leading men to get up what they have called a land monopoly ticket at the elections. This has caused some to believe that the extensive land claimants and wealthy will in some way or other use this vigilance committee to favor their own selfish ends. We do not know whether these fears are groundless or otherwise, but the truth is the committee no longer has the bone and sinew of this community with it, and it is safe to infer that no executions will again be made by its authority. That the vigilance committee is losing the confidence of leading men, and becoming the subject of suspicion and vituperation, is not to be wondered at. The only marvel is that such despotic and dangerous power has been permitted to establish itself upon its present basis. But what will follow this reaction of public sentiment? Will the members of the committee themselves be safe from reprisals? May the same people who delighted when the committee took prisoners from the city jail and gave an exhibition of a double execution on the Sabbath, may this populace take its second thought and join the authorities in demanding from the committee the evidence of its legal right to condemn and hang for crimes which the constitution does not punish with death? And how is the committee prepared for such a day of reckoning? It is one thing to suspend a man from a beam and jerk him up and down until he is killed, as in the above Sunday execution, amid the howlings of a gratified mob, and it is another and widely different thing to face a stern, properly constituted, legal tribunal which, by the silent but unceasing operation of a great principle, has recovered its authority with the people, and can now punish those who assumed its powers and exercised, and even exceeded, its prerogatives.

spellchecked_text: Our Journal, and forwarded through Adams & Co. or Gregory's Express, will be attended to without delay. Lynch Law—Three Indians Executed. Judge Lynch has recently been holding his session in the western part of our county. He has pursued quite a different course in his official career to that of his contemporaries, and sometimes, perhaps not unjustly; though we hope the time has passed, when it can be said such things are necessary for the protection of the lives and property of our citizens, except in extreme cases. The hindrance has been, when it was almost impossible, in consequence of the growing character of our population, to convict a man of any crime by the regular courts of justice, it being impossible to obtain witnesses. But another consideration once combined with this to excite these summary calls of justice. We were assembled from all parts of the world, strangers, and almost unknown to each other, and unless a villain were apprehended and executed himself in the act of his crime, his identity could scarcely be proven in after time. But these and other excuses for such summary proceedings are fast vanishing before the rapid improvements of our society. And it were better to bear with a little evil in the tardy workings of judicial operations, than to risk the great liability of an excited multitude doing injustice to innocent persons suspected of crime. No one will doubt the correctness of the intentions of those engaging in those summary executions; but all who have observed their operations in California for the last two years must have observed their great liability to err, and the difficulty with which their excited tempers can be controlled when once public feeling has set in against an individual. Some two or three weeks since, two men named Ross and Pope were apprehended at Newtown for stealing, and not being able to get evidence enough even to have them bound over for trial, one of them was sentenced to be hung, for the avowed purpose of making him confess the crime, but through the timely interference of Messrs. McConnell, Endicott, and others, he was rescued. On Monday last, another man was arrested for stealing; in which case we do not know the character of the evidence; but he was sentenced to receive a few lashes, which sentence was duly executed. In addition to those, we have received the following communication—the detail of another execution: "At a court held on the 1st day of June, 1852, at Wilson's ranch, by the inhabitants residing in the vicinity, for the trial of Yalla, Leno, Camerock, and Hoosppa, four Indians charged with the murder of Martin Hopkins, on the 1st day of June, 1852. On motion, K. McDowell was appointed Judge, James C. Murdoch Clerk, O. Evans attorney for the people, and Samuel S. Gentilins counsel for the prisoners. The following persons, to wit: C. C. Williams, A. G. Cole, J. J. Runks, Wm. H. Knowles, C. Musgrove, Geo. Baller, Jas. Rathbun, L. P. Poor, W. X. Farber, and N. S. Chaplin, were sworn and empaneled a jury for the trial of the prisoners, who, having heard the evidence—as well on the part of the people as the prisoners—retired a short distance, and after some time returned with the following verdict: "We, the jury, find the defendants Yalla, Leno, and Hocapa guilty, and adjudge that they be at once executed by hanging. No evidence being adduced against the defendant Camerock, we therefore find him not guilty." We do not sit in judgment to condemn the acts of this court and jury. The sentence, we are informed, was duly executed. The trial and execution was done all upon the instant, without giving the mind that time necessary to sober down after an excitement, and look at the circumstances with an unprejudiced eye. The man who will never form unjust conclusions in this way, approximates perfection to a degree not allowed to the great body of human beings; for we are all creatures of passion and prejudices, and he who will never act is almost invariably hasty.

The country below this and north of the Illinois River has been for a long time and is now infested with a gang of blacklegs, counterfeiters, horse thieves and land pirates, and the good people have found our laws, or at least the administration of them, entirely inadequate to the protection of their property. Consequently, they have been forced to form themselves into "volunteer companies and anti-horse thief societies." One was formed about 20 miles below this, at Washington Grove. Mr. Campbell was actively engaged in such efforts when, in June, two of the Driskells, notorious throughout this region as ringleaders and harborers of all sorts of villains, rode up to Campbell's house and asked his son if his father was at home. He called his father to the door, when the Driskells shot him dead, and fled. The volunteer companies of DeKalb and Winnebago Counties immediately collected and went in search of the Driskells. On Tuesday they caught the old man and one of his sons; tried them by Lynch law, and were convinced that they were the cause, if not the perpetrators, of the atrocious murder of Mr. Campbell. High-handed and revolting as this summary mode of procedure seems to be, it is, nevertheless, absolutely necessary, and receives the commendation of every individual who is at all acquainted with the facts. If a man refuses to join these companies, he is at once put down with the horse thieves.

article: OGLE CŒUN' Y- LYNCH LAW.- The Attorney General of the state of Illinois, Mr. Lamborn, has published an opinion rela tive to the recent exercise of the lynch law in Ogle county, in the case of the Driscalls. Mr. Lamborn regards the sum mary execution of the horse thieves, as wholly unjustifiable and uncalled for in the exigencies of the case. He says," I have no doubt that when the indignation and phrenzy of the occasion, shall have passed away, the actors in the general tragedy will join in the general lamentation, which must pervade society wherever the bloody details are made known." He contends that the laws of Illinois, are sufficiently rigid and fully adequate to any emergency. Nearly thirty persons have been sentenced to the penitentiary within the last year, from the stricts infected with the horse thieves and blacklegs. The plea there fore that the arm of the law is too weak, to bring offenders to justice, is wholly without foundation. The prosecutions in the northern counties of Illinois have been nusually severe, as is proved by the num ber of prisoners sent to the penitentiary, from the very district of country, suppos d to be under the control of a gang of des peradocs.-

article: ILLINOIS LYNCH LAW --- Since our ac count of last week, with regard to the lynch ing tragedy in Ogle Co., Illinois, we have received conflicting and contradictory state ments through the papers, of the circum stances connected with that transaction. --- From all that we are able to learn, it would seem the mers prudent portion of the peo ple, are far from justifying the summary trial and execution of the two Driscalls, for the alleged murder of John Campbell. A Coroners inquest has been held upon the bodies of the Driscalls, and the jury have returned a verdict of wilful murder! This then, is likely to result in serious business to those who assumed to take the law into their own hands. We learn that immediately after the mob had wreaked their vengeance upon the lives of two Driscalls, they repaired to the residences of all the Driscalls and expelled the widowed and orphaned families, and burnt their houses to the ground. It is al so stated that money and valuable papers, were upon the persons of the Driscalls at the time of their being shot, which were abstracted from their pockets by the mob. The Driscalls were the owners valu- ble farms, which are under a high of state of cultivation, and covered with extensive crops of growing grain. The mob have forbidden under the penalty of death any persons from harvesting the crops. Bridge, whom we stated last week as being one of the murderers o" Campbell, has been arrested, tried, and acquitted. We learn from the Galena papers, that the of- fice of the Rockford Star," was entered by the mob on the night of the 6th instant, and the type and fixtures so much injured and mutulated, that the paper has been obliged to discontinue. The alleged cause for this transaction is, that the Star has spoken out in condemnation of the proceed ings of the mob. In a good government Lynch Law can never be justified. Lynch Law is the stepping stone to anarchy, misrule and un controlable violence. To say that the laws of the states, are inadequate to perform the demands of human justice, is a libel upon our government and institutions. It is a foul charge, which the enemies of republicanism in Europe, have ever attempted to fasten upon us, but one which we in theory have ever repudiated and denied. The lynchers of the Driscalls, plead in just- ification that the friends of good order, were too weak to enforce the law, and bring the offenders to merited justice .--- This cannot be true. The same power which was brought into requisition to bring the Driscalls before a lynch tribunal, was amply adequate to have brought them be fore a legal court of the State of Illinois. The laws of Illinois for the apprehension, conviction, and punishment of felons and murderers, are as speedy and as rigid in any other State in the Union. as

article: RIOT IN CINCINNATI, OHIO. A Letter to the editors of the New York New Era, from Cincinnati, Ohio, dated the 4th inst. gives an account of a very serious riot in that city. On the evening of the 2d, a quarrel occurred between several negroes and two white men, in which the latter were badly wounded with dirk knives. A bout 9 o'clock on the following evening, a large concourse of people, without concert or arms, assembled in the immediate vicinity of" Five Points," or, as it is called," Nigger Town." A few persons in the mob which consisted of 3 or 400, threw stones against the buildings of the negroes. The negroes immediately poured into the mob a volley of bullets, from muskets and rifles, with which they had previously provided themselves in anticipation of an attack. The mob, being unarmed, fled precipitate ly, and were pursued for nearly a square by the blacks, who yelled out a wild shout of triumph and defiance, and returned to their houses. About midnight the mob advanced to the position they had occupied in the early part of the evening, provided with arms and a six- pounder. The six pounder and small arms were fired, which was re turned by the blacks, and the parties engaged in a terrible conflict. Fortunately for the lives of many, the prompt arrival of the military silenced the firing, restored peace and dispersed the mob. There are various reports of the number killed and wounded on both sides, the truth of which cannot at pres ent be known. The city was all in confusion and uproar again, on the 4th, and the negroes flying in all directions. There was no fighting or lynching, but the people were taking the negroes into custody as fast as they could be caught, with the design of enforcing a law which requires all colored residents of Ohio to give bond for their good or leave the State. behavior

article: MORE LYNCH LAW .--- Two men named Couch and Maythe, were lynched at Willi. amstown, Grant county, Ky, last Saturday week, for committing a murderous assault up. on a drover, named Utterbeck, whom they also robbed. The mob went to the jail in which they were confined, took them out by force, carried them to the epot where they had committed the outrage on the drover, and hung them both upon a tree. The mob seeme to have acted with the utmost order in this ehocking tragedy, and even listened with respect to the remonstrance of an eminent law yer against their proceedings. spellchecked_text: Miscellaneous. From the Natchitoches Herald. TEXAS. Murder—Lynch Law—Last of the Yoakum Gang. We have been put in possession of the facts in relation to this affair, which is one among the last Texas tragedies. The citizens of Jefferson County, it appears, have long suffered from their outrages; and from their numbers and total recklessness of character, it seemed impossible to arrest their injuries by the hand of civil power. Cattle had been stolen, robberies committed, and citizens insulted and murdered; but still, whenever any were arrested on the charge, the gang came forward with perjured oaths, and they were acquitted. "Yoakum" was hardened into the most inveterate degree of crime, and seemed but to reap enjoyment by pursuing the most fiendish acts of robbery and murder. It is a most singular instance of the effects of habit. He was a rich and affluent planter, and lived in a sumptuous and most magnificent manner—kept a splendid equipage—owned over a hundred negroes and large tracts of land—had constantly about a hundred breeding mares, made a yearly sale of fifteen hundred cattle, and had a large revenue coming from other sources. There is no doubt that he was the richest man in Texas. Yet with all this wealth, his disposition to plunder knew no bounds. The cause of his death arose from an abortive attempt to murder Mr. Carey of Houston County.—Mr. C. is a highly respectable and wealthy citizen of the town of Houston, and was at the time staying at the residence of Yoakum. He was suspected of having a large sum of money with him, and Yoakum determined that he should be murdered while in bed. The plan was properly managed during the day, and everything placed in readiness for the commission. Nothing remained but the darkness of the night.
